questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct article: He is _____ entirely honest man.

options.option_text: a (alternative interpretation)
an
the
no article

questions.explanation: Although 'entirely' begins with a vowel sound, let's look at the phrase. 'entirely honest man'. The word immediately following the article is 'entirely', which starts with a vowel sound /ɪ/. So 'an' is correct. If the blank was before 'honest', 'honest' also starts with a vowel sound ('o'), taking 'an'.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct article: _____ bright sun strictly rises in the east.

options.option_text: A (alternative interpretation)
An (alternative interpretation)
The
No article

questions.explanation: The definite article 'The' is used before unique universal objects like the sun, the moon, the sky, the earth, etc.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct article: I unexpectedly saw _____ one-eyed old man crossing the busy road.

options.option_text: an
the
no article
a

questions.explanation: The word 'one' begins with a consonant sound 'w' (wun). Therefore, the indefinite article 'a' is used before it, not 'an'.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct article: _____ Pure gold is an extremely precious and valuable metal.

options.option_text: No article
A (alternative interpretation)
An (alternative interpretation)
The (alternative interpretation)

questions.explanation: Uncountable material nouns (like gold, silver, water, iron) do not take any article when they are used in a general or universal sense.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct article: He brilliantly plays _____ wooden flute beautifully every evening.

options.option_text: a (alternative interpretation)
an (alternative interpretation)
the
no article

questions.explanation: The definite article 'the' is conventionally used before the names of musical instruments when referring to playing them.

questions.stem: Fill in the blanks with the correct articles: _____ more you actively read, _____ better you truly understand.

options.option_text: A, a (alternative interpretation)
The, the
The, a (alternative interpretation)
No article, no article

questions.explanation: The structure 'The + comparative adjective ..., the + comparative adjective ...' is used to show that two things change or happen together (parallel increase or decrease).

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct article: After the long meeting, she was formally appointed _____ Principal of the renowned college.

options.option_text: the (alternative interpretation)
a (alternative interpretation)
an (alternative interpretation)
no article

questions.explanation: We typically omit the article before a noun that represents a unique position or title, especially after verbs like appoint, elect, declare, make, and crown.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The Nile is considered _____ longest river in the world by most historical geographers.

options.option_text: a — used before singular countable nouns in general
an — used before words beginning with a vowel sound
the — compulsory before superlative adjectives always
no article is required before descriptive adjectives

questions.explanation: 'The' is mandatory before superlative adjectives (longest, tallest, best). Options A/B ('a'/'an') are indefinite and cannot be used with superlatives, which by definition identify a unique entity. Option D is incorrect because articles routinely precede adjective-noun phrases.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: She has been learning _____ violin since childhood and now performs at national-level competitions.

options.option_text: a — indefinite article for singular countable nouns
the — definite article always used before musical instruments
an — indefinite article for nouns with vowel-sound starts
no article is needed before names of instruments here

questions.explanation: In English, 'the' is used before names of musical instruments when referring to learning or playing them (play the guitar, learn the violin, practise the flute). Option D is a very common error; omitting the article before instrument names is grammatically incorrect in this construction.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank with the correct article: He had _____ lunch with his senior colleagues at the new restaurant near Parliament Street.

options.option_text: the — definite article for a specific and known meal
a — indefinite article for singular countable nouns used
an — indefinite article used before nouns with vowel sounds
no article — unmodified meal names in general use take none

questions.explanation: Names of meals used in a general, unmodified sense (breakfast, lunch, dinner, tea) take no article. 'The' would only be correct with specific reference (e.g., 'the lunch he described'). An article becomes necessary only when the meal noun is modified (e.g., 'a working lunch', 'a lavish dinner').

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: The sub-inspector confirmed that _____ FIR had been registered against the accused at the local police station.

options.option_text: a — FIR starts with the consonant letter F in spelling
an — FIR is pronounced /ef-aɪ-ɑːr/, opening with vowel /ɛ/
the — FIR is a specific document referenced in the context
no article — government legal documents do not need articles

questions.explanation: Article choice is governed by pronunciation, not spelling. FIR is pronounced as individual letters: /ɛf-aɪ-ɑːr/; the first sound is the vowel /ɛ/, so 'an' is required. Option A confuses the written letter F with its spoken sound. Option C ('the') would only apply if FIR had been specifically introduced earlier in the conversation.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: _____ number of candidates who cleared the UPSC Prelims this year was the lowest in over a decade.

options.option_text: A — 'a number of' means several and is a very common phrase
An — the word 'number' begins with the consonant letter n
The — 'the number of' denotes a specific count, taking singular verb
No article — abstract quantity expressions never take articles

questions.explanation: 'The number of + plural noun' is treated as singular and refers to a definite, specific count — consistent with the singular verb 'was' in the sentence. 'A number of + plural noun' means 'several' and requires a plural verb (e.g., 'A number of candidates were absent'). Using 'A' here with 'was' would be grammatically incorrect.

questions.stem: Fill in the blank: _____ determination she showed while recovering from her injury inspired every athlete in the national training camp.

options.option_text: A — first mention of an uncountable noun may take indefinite
An — 'determination' begins with a vowel so needs an here
The — specifies a particular instance of an abstract quality
No article — abstract nouns categorically never take any article

questions.explanation: Abstract nouns (determination, wisdom, courage) take 'the' when the context identifies a specific, particularised instance — here, 'she showed' pins the determination to one person at one time. Option D states an absolute falsehood; abstract nouns frequently take 'the' in specific contexts. Option A is wrong because 'a determination' implies a countable meaning ('a resolve/decision'), which distorts the intended sense.

questions.stem: Which of the following sentences uses articles CORRECTLY throughout?

options.option_text: She is best student in her batch and won an university gold medal
He rented a one-bedroom apartment in an European capital last year
The verdict was announced after the jury deliberated for an hour
She displayed a great courage at the front, earning an honour roll spot

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'the jury' (specific group), 'an hour' (hour = /aʊər/, vowel sound). Option A fails twice: superlative 'best' requires 'the best', and 'university' (/juːnɪ-/) opens with consonant /j/, needing 'a', not 'an'. Option B: 'European' (/jʊərə-/) also opens with /j/, so 'a European', not 'an'. Option D: 'courage' is uncountable and cannot take the indefinite 'a'; the sentence needs either 'great courage' or 'extraordinary courage'.
